questions.question: In the context of batch learning in neural networks, does the order in which input data is presented to the network influence the learning process?

options.A: Yes, the order significantly affects learning, leading to different models.
options.B: No, the order of input data does not influence the learning outcome in batch learning.
options.C: Yes, but only in networks with more than three layers.
options.D: The order only matters in real-time data streaming, not in batch learning.

questions.answer: (B) No, the order of input data does not influence the learning outcome in batch learning. In batch learning, the entire dataset is considered in one go, or in large batches, for the training process.

questions.question: What impact will increasing the number of nodes in a neural network's hidden layer have?

options.A: It will always improve the network's accuracy on both training and test sets.
options.B: It may lead to underfitting, resulting in poor accuracy on both training and test sets.
options.C: It may result in overfitting, leading to higher accuracy on the training set but poor accuracy on the test set, and increased training time.
options.D: The number of nodes in the hidden layer has no impact on the network's performance.

questions.answer: (C) It may result in overfitting, leading to higher accuracy on the training set but poor accuracy on the test set and increased training time.

questions.question: You are designing a deep learning system to detect driver fatigue in cars, where it is crucial to detect fatigue accurately to prevent accidents. Which of the following evaluation metrics would be the most appropriate for this system?
questions.answer: (B) Recall. Recall is the most appropriate metric in this context because it measures the proportion of actual positive cases (fatigue detected) that were correctly identified.

questions.question: Assuming δL/δx3 is known, write the weight update for δL/δw1 (should be in the expanded form). Input x1 and all weights are positive. All neurons have ReLU Activation. Given ∂y1/∂z1 = ∂x2/∂z2 = ∂y2/∂z3 = ∂x3/∂z4 = 1.
Consider an activation function ρ(x)=x·σ(x), where σ(x) is the sigmoid function. (a) Compute ρ'(x) in terms of σ(x). (b) For large x, compare ρ(x) and ρ'(x) with standard activation functions.

options.a: Compute ρ'(x) in terms of σ(x).
options.b: For large x, compare ρ(x) and ρ'(x) with standard activation functions.

questions.answer: (a) ρ'(x) = σ(x)[1 + x(1 − σ(x))]. (b) For large values of x, σ(x) ≈ 1, thus ρ(x) ≈ x (mimics ReLU) and ρ'(x) mimics Sigmoid activation.

questions.question: Consider an ensemble of 5 models which are trained on the same architecture but have different initializations for a handwritten digit classification task. Does the guarantee of better performance in expectation (in terms of cross-entropy loss) by averaging the predictions of all five networks hold if you instead average the weights and biases of the networks? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No, the guarantee does not hold because the loss is not convex with respect to the weights and biases. Networks starting from different initializations might learn different hidden representations.

questions.question: Prove that approximately 63% of the entire original dataset (total training set) is present in any of the sampled bootstrap datasets using the Bagging method.
questions.answer: Probability of an observation not being chosen in one draw is 1 − 1/n. For n draws, it is (1 − 1/n)^n. As n → ∞, this limit is e^−1 ≈ 0.368. Probability of appearing is 1 − 0.368 = 0.632 (approx 63%).

questions.question: Enumerate and explain the desirable properties of a distance metric. Evaluate the Canberra distance d(x,y) = Σ |x_i − y_i| / |x_i + y_i| against these properties.
questions.answer: Properties: Symmetry (D(A,B)=D(B,A)), Positivity (D(A,B) ≥ 0, 0 iff A=B), and Triangle Inequality. Canberra distance exhibits symmetry and positivity but fails the triangle inequality.

questions.question: Discuss the role of activation functions in mitigating exploding and vanishing gradient problems. Provide examples.
questions.answer: Sigmoid and tanh are prone to vanishing gradients because their derivatives are small. ReLU, Leaky ReLU, and ELU alleviate vanishing gradients by having a constant gradient for positive inputs.

questions.question: If you forget to divide activations by keep-probability p in dropout during training, how to fix at test time?
questions.answer: At test time, multiply outputs of each layer by p. Since dropout was off, expected activation is larger by factor 1/p; scaling by p restores the expected value.

questions.question: What is the difference between a model and an algorithm? Give one example.
questions.answer: A model is the output of the training process. It represents the learned patterns or relationships in terms of parameters from the data. A model is what you use to make predictions or inferences on new data after training... An algorithm, on the other hand, is the procedure or set of rules used to optimize and train the model. Example: Model is y=wx+b, Algorithm is Gradient Descent.

questions.question: The logistic S-curve is non-linear. Why do we still call the Logistic Regression a Linear model?
questions.answer: The term "linear" refers to the fact that the model's prediction is based on a linear combination of input features (b1x1 + ... + b0). The logistic function maps this linear combination to a probability, but the underlying decision boundary is linear in the feature space.

questions.question: What is the difference between simple and multiple regression?
questions.answer: Simple regression involves a single independent variable (feature) to predict the dependent variable. Multiple regression involves two or more independent variables.

questions.question: What is the difference between knowledge-based learning (KBL) and feedback-based learning (FBL)? Give an example of an FBL model that is also a KBL model.
questions.answer: Knowledge-Based Learning involves systems learning from established knowledge/rules. Feedback-Based Learning improves through feedback (supervised/reinforcement). Decision Tree and Bayesian Networks are both FBL and KBL models.

questions.question: What is PET in the context of ML?

questions.question: Explain in detail the difference between MLE, MCLE and MAP methods.
